prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 as an incretin hormone and the identification of its active form, which made incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity possible

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: a single-part prize on B033 for Holst, Drucker and Mojsov. The round-1 exchange strengthened rather than weakened the scientific case. Six independent statements describe the same chain: GLP-1 as a gut incretin that potentiates glucose-dependent insulin secretion, the identity of the active truncated peptide, receptor biology, and then large randomized trials showing benefit in glycaemia, weight, cardiovascular and renal outcomes. No one argued that the work is immature. As a physician-scientist in autoimmunity I value a discovery in which mechanism and patient benefit are both demonstrated, and few on the shortlist meet that bar. Defining the prize around the physiology and the active peptide, and not around the pharmaceutical optimisation that followed, gives the committee a claim it can state precisely and defend. I also see no reason to defer: the open points on long-term safety and durability in obesity are about refinement of use, not about whether the discovery is real.
statement.case_against: Attribution remains the weakness and I should not hide that my confidence in the exact trio is lower than my confidence in the achievement. Mojsov's priority for identifying the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide against Habener and colleagues, who are not credited, cannot be resolved from the supplied text, so a trio containing her could be challenged. Excluding Knudsen can be read as a judgement against translation even though liraglutide and semaglutide are what patients receive, and any three-name cut leaves out real contributors. If the committee concluded that the Mojsov question is genuinely unsettled, the configuration would be at risk, and I would then prefer a narrower, better-supported credit or a different ballot over a name added as a compromise.

responses.point: As chair you asked whether the primary literature supports crediting Mojsov over Habener's group, and what citation wording avoids implying a first discovery of the incretin concept.
responses.response: I cannot answer the priority question from the supplied evidence, and I do not want to pretend the unanimity of the trio resolves it. What I can say is that the citation can be written so that it does not depend on resolving it: it names GLP-1 as an incretin hormone, which rests on Holst and Drucker, and speaks of identification of the active form, not of its first discovery. That wording credits Mojsov for a specific, verifiable contribution (identification and synthesis of the active peptide) and leaves room for the committee to examine Habener's earlier work before the vote. I agree with your observation that the open work is the names and the wording, and not whether to recognise the discovery. I also note your point that you do not think the evidence supports waiting, and I agree.

responses.point: You would fall back to Drucker and Holst only, without an industrial name, if the committee judges the Mojsov evidence unresolved.
responses.response: I think that is the principled fallback, and I prefer it to restoring Knudsen as an automatic substitute. My opening ballot put Knudsen in the third place, and I withdrew that in round 1 because it changes the nature of the prize. A two-person prize on B033 would be narrower but defensible, and it is better than a third name chosen to fill the slot. Where I differ slightly is on timing of that decision: if the committee can consult the primary papers before voting and finds Mojsov's contribution supportable, which is my working assumption, the trio should stand, and I would not pre-emptively drop her on the basis of a contested priority claim alone.

responses.point: You regard B036 (Mori and Walter) as the cleaner two-person alternative on attribution grounds if B033's credit is judged unfair or unsettled, though with weaker clinical impact.
responses.response: I agree with this ordering and it is why B036 is my first alternative. The mechanism is beyond question and the credit is tidy. My concern, which you share, is that therapeutic modulation of the unfolded protein response has not yet yielded a validated treatment, so I would only move there if B033 truly failed on attribution, not merely because its credit is imperfect. Every large prize has some contested edge, and a clean list should not outweigh demonstrated benefit to patients. I also keep B013 as the second alternative, because June and Sadelain are a clear pair, but that needs a careful argument about Rosenberg and Eshhar.

responses.point: You say the mechanistic bridge to therapy, confirmed independently and in randomized trials, is rarer than a drug approval alone, and you doubt whether a second achievement such as B047 or B011 can be added.
responses.response: I agree with the first point, and it is the reason the physiology-centred framing does not undervalue the clinical impact: the drugs exist because the mechanism was understood. On a second part, I do not see room for one. B033 needs three names to be coherent, so a second achievement would force a cut of one of Holst, Drucker or Mojsov, which would make the GLP-1 credit weaker. I would rather give the committee one clean part than split the recognition. B047 is an interesting field and I would revisit it in a later year, when antisense therapy has a longer record.

uncertainties: Whether the primary literature supports crediting Mojsov for identification of the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide against Habener and colleagues; I cannot resolve this from the supplied evidence.
Whether the committee will accept a physiology-only definition of the prize that leaves out Knudsen, or will read it as a judgement against translation.
Whether a two-name fallback (Holst and Drucker) would still be seen as complete if the Mojsov question remained open at the time of the vote.
Long-term safety and durability of GLP-1 agents in obesity, which I do not think should delay recognition but which are still accumulating.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with any credited name on the shortlist is apparent from my profile. My research is in autoimmunity, so I have a topical interest in immunology candidates such as the cGAS-STING pathway (B039) and in the CAR-T ballot (B013), but that is not a personal or institutional tie, and neither ballot is in my preferred configuration. My round-1 disclosure stands unchanged.
